title: Ὁδοιπόρος καὶ Ἀλήθεια
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 259 (= Perry 355). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὁδοιπορῶν τις ἐν ἐρήμῳ εὗρε γυναῖκα μόνην κατηφῆ ἑστῶσαν, καί φησιν αὐτῇ· « Τίς εἶ ; »
sentences.tr: Hodoiporōn tis en erēmōi heure gynaika monēn katēphē hestōsan, kai phēsin autēi· « Tis ei ; »
sentences.l: Someone travelling in a wilderness found a woman standing alone and downcast, and he says to her: « Who are you? »
sentences.n: φησίν is the historic present, dropped into a past narrative for immediacy; Greek does this freely and English does not. ἑστῶσαν is the perfect participle of ἵστημι with present force, 'standing'. The mark that closes the question is the Greek semicolon, and the space before it is Chambry's French printing habit, kept as part of his page.

The quotation opens here and does not close until the end of the traveller's next question: Chambry sets one pair of guillemets around this two-turn exchange and marks the change of speaker with a dash. A sentence with an opening « and no closing » is therefore correct here, not an error.

sentences.t: — Καὶ διὰ ποίαν αἰτίαν τὴν πόλιν ἀφεῖσα τὴν ἐρημίαν οἰκεῖς ; »
sentences.tr: — Kai dia poian aitian tēn polin apheisa tēn erēmian oikeis ; »
sentences.l: — And for what reason, having left the city, do you inhabit the wilderness? »
sentences.n: The dash is Chambry's mark for the change of speaker; the traveller is talking again. ἀφεῖσα is the aorist participle of ἀφίημι, feminine, agreeing with the woman: 'having let the city go'.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ εἶπεν· « Ὅτι τοῖς πάλαι καιροῖς παρ’ ὀλίγοις ἦν τὸ ψεῦδος· νῦν δὲ εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους ἐστίν, ἐάν τι ἀκούειν καὶ λέγειν θέλῃς. »
sentences.tr: Hē de eipen· « Hoti tois palai kairois par’ oligois ēn to pseudos· nyn de eis pantas anthrōpous estin, ean ti akouein kai legein thelēis. »
sentences.l: And she said: « Because in the times of old the lie was among few; but now it is out among all men, if you should wish to hear and to say anything. »
sentences.i: And she said: « Because in the old days falsehood was with only a few; but now it has gone out to all men, if there is anything at all you care to hear and to say. »
sentences.n: Ὅτι here is causal, 'because', answering διὰ ποίαν αἰτίαν — not the declarative ὅτι that opens so many of this collection's morals. The two prepositions are set against each other: παρά with the dative puts falsehood beside a few people, while εἰς with the accusative gives spread, out into all of them. ἐάν with the subjunctive θέλῃς makes the condition a general one.

sentences.t: Ὅτι κάκιστος βίος καὶ πονηρὸς τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐστίν, ὅτε τὸ ψεῦδος προκρίνεται τῆς ἀληθείας.
sentences.tr: Hoti kakistos bios kai ponēros tois anthrōpois estin, hote to pseudos prokrinetai tēs alētheias.
sentences.l: That life is most evil and wretched for men, when the lie is preferred to the truth.
sentences.i: The story shows that life is most evil and wretched for men when the lie is preferred to the truth.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι, 'that', with nothing to govern it: the introducing verb is left unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. προκρίνω is to choose one thing before another, and the genitive τῆς ἀληθείας names the thing passed over.
